issues.legal_issue: A plaintiff’s readiness and willingness to perform a contract may be established by pleadings read as a whole and need not be expressed in prescribed words.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement to sell and stated in the plaint that she had throughout been ready and willing to complete the sale.
The plaintiff also led evidence concerning her readiness and willingness to perform her part of the agreement.
The trial court and the first appellate court found in the plaintiff’s favour.
issues.conclusion: The pleadings and evidence sufficiently established readiness and willingness; the High Court erred in finding that the requirement was not met merely because the plaint did not use a particular form of words.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with its explanations, requires the plaintiff to aver and prove that she has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms to be performed by her. The pleading is read as a whole for its substance, not tested by a mechanical requirement for particular words. The Court relied on Ardeshir H. Mama v. Flora Sassoon, Prem Raj v. D.L.F. Housing and Construction (P) Ltd., Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, Motilal Jain v. Ramdasi Devi, Surya Narain Upadhyaya v. Ram Roop Pandey, and Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaint_read_as_a_whole_shows_readiness: The plaintiff’s pleadings, read as a whole, conveyed readiness and willingness to perform her contractual obligations.
predicates.evidence_supports_readiness: The plaintiff presented evidence supporting her readiness and willingness to perform her contractual obligations.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff seeks specific performance and the pleadings as a whole convey readiness supported by evidence, the readiness and willingness requirement is satisfied without any need for prescribed wording.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance is timely when no date for performance was fixed and it was brought within three years after the plaintiff had notice that performance was refused.
material_facts: No date for performance was fixed in the agreement relied on by the plaintiff.
The plaintiff received notice in July 1978 that the property had been sold to others.
The plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance on 3 January 1979.
issues.conclusion: The suit was within time because it was filed within three years after the plaintiff had notice of the refusal of performance.
issues.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provides a three-year limitation period for a suit for specific performance, running from the date fixed for performance or, if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.no_performance_date_fixed: The parties did not fix a date for performance of the contract.
predicates.suit_filed_within_three_years_of_notice_: The plaintiff filed the suit within three years after learning that the other party had refused performance.

issues.definition: A specific-performance suit is timely if no performance date was fixed and the plaintiff filed it within three years after learning of the refusal to perform.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may not disturb concurrent factual findings in a second appeal unless a legally recognized basis for interference is present, such as perversity or a conclusion contrary to the evidence or settled law.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court found that the subsequent purchasers were not bona fide purchasers without notice and recorded findings of collusion and knowledge of the earlier agreement.
The first appellate court examined the evidence concerning the purchasers’ knowledge in detail.
The High Court reversed those factual findings without material supporting the reversal and addressed matters that had not been framed as issues in the suit.
The Supreme Court found the High Court’s decision indefensible and restored the trial court’s decree as affirmed by the first appellate court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the permissible scope of a second appeal by disturbing supported concurrent findings without a proper basis for interference; its judgment was set aside and the lower courts’ judgment and decree were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, permits a second appeal only where a substantial question of law is involved and requires the High Court to formulate that question, subject to the statutory proviso. Concurrent findings of fact cannot be disturbed merely because another view is possible; interference requires a recognized legal basis, such as findings that are perverse, unsupported by evidence, or contrary to mandatory law or settled legal principles. The Court relied on Sir Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Ltd. v. Century Spinning & Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Reserve Bank of India v. Ramkrishna Govind Morey, and Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitribai Sopan Gujar.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and not findings_perverse

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal from a civil judgment.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual findings.
predicates.findings_perverse: The lower courts’ findings are shown to be perverse, unsupported by the record, or contrary to applicable mandatory law.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, concurrent factual findings that are not shown to be perverse must remain undisturbed.
